subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Availability Heuristic
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Availability Heuristic.

hook.text: After a plane crash on the news, people drive instead of fly. Driving is far more dangerous. Why the switch?

buildup.text: The availability heuristic: we judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind.

discovery.text: Vivid, recent, or emotional events are easier to recall—so we overestimate how common they are.

twist.text: Shark attacks get news coverage. Falling coconuts don't. Coconuts kill more people every year.

climax.text: Doctors misdiagnose when a rare disease was in last week's journal. Recency warps clinical judgment.

punchline.text: Easy to recall doesn't mean likely to happen.

quiz.question: What drives the availability heuristic?
options: How easily examples come to mind

details.summary: People estimate the likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind rather than actual statistics. Vivid, recent, or emotionally charged events are recalled more readily, making them seem more common. This availability heuristic distorts risk assessment systematically.
details.whyItMatters: The availability heuristic explains why people overestimate rare dramatic risks like plane crashes and underestimate common ones like heart disease. Media coverage amplifies the distortion.
takeaways: Ease of recall is mistaken for frequency or probability
Vivid and recent events are overweighted in risk judgments

faq.question: How does media coverage affect the availability heuristic?
faq.answer: Media disproportionately covers dramatic, unusual events like terrorist attacks and shark attacks. This floods memory with vivid examples, making these events seem more common than they are. Meanwhile, common killers like diabetes receive less coverage and seem less threatening.

faq.question: How can you counteract the availability heuristic?
faq.answer: Seek base rate statistics rather than relying on examples that come to mind. Ask whether your impression might be shaped by recent news or personal experience rather than reality. Deliberately consider events that are harder to recall to balance your assessment.
